BREAKING: The S&P GSCI Agriculture Index has now risen for 11 consecutive trading sessions, matching a similar streak last seen in 1994.

The gauge tracks a broad basket of agricultural commodities, including wheat, corn, soybeans, sugar, coffee, cotton, cocoa and livestock.

Over this span, the index has surged +13.4%, to its highest level since July 2023.

Over the last 125 years, only 5 periods have seen the index rise for more than 11 consecutive sessions, most recently in the 1930s.

Meanwhile, wheat prices have soared +22.9% so far in August, to $7.84 per bushel, their highest since February 2023.

Food inflation pressures are intensifying.

Cardboard box demand is one of the cleanest reads on the real goods economy. E-commerce was supposed to send it to the moon.

Instead, US box shipments per capita just hit a record low, below where they were in 1999. Southern pine pulpwood now fetches a 40-year low, and in some places growers are paying to have their timber hauled off rather than getting paid for it.

Amazon shrank its boxes, plastic mailers took share, and recycled and Brazilian pulp displaced domestic wood. The demand that was supposed to boom went the other way. A forest economy 6 million landowners depend on is in crisis, and the read under the e-commerce hype is simple: real goods demand is weaker than the headlines say.

tweets.text:
The last time the market churned like this was 1901.

NYSE turnover hit 319% that year, the entire market changing hands every 16 weeks, a velocity Wall Street would not match again for more than a century. Today's version is 0DTE options: more than 3 million same-day S&P 500 contracts trade every day, next to prediction markets, 100-to-1 perps, and a $1 trillion SpaceX IPO.

The 1901 fever ran hot for years before it broke. Then came the Panic of 1907 and a 30% crash, 10% of it in a single October. Velocity like this is the signature of a speculative blowoff. It can run for a while, and every prior one ended the same way, with the people holding cash buying the wreckage from the people who were sure it was different.

🇨🇳 🌎 China may be winning the global industrial battle while destroying part of the profitability of its own companies - Nikkei

📉 Chinese companies are trapped in such intense competition that they have to invest more, expand capacity, accelerate technologically and cut prices simply to avoid being overtaken. This has created global leaders in EVs, batteries, solar and electronics but at the cost of enormous pressure on margins. For example, Chinese manufacturers exported 2.3 million vehicles in H1 2026, almost as many as in the whole of 2025, yet sector profits still fell 20% while margins dropped to just 3.8% from 8% in 2017. Domestic demand is no longer absorbing enough of that production capacity, so Chinese companies are looking abroad for growth.

⚔️ However, exports are not necessarily less profitable as Geely says it can make 12,000 to 15,000 yuan of profit on an exported car vs. less than 3,000 yuan in China. Profitability can gradually disappear if all Chinese manufacturers enter the same foreign markets and reproduce the domestic price war abroad. China’s trade surplus, which exceeded $1 trillion in 2025, obviously reflects tremendous competitiveness but also a deeper macro imbalance. Therefore, an increasing share of the rest of the world is being asked to absorb what China does not consume itself, and that has a major consequence for the global economy.

⚠️ When Chinese companies are willing to accept extremely thin margins to gain volume, they force foreign competitors to cut prices or sacrifice margins. Goldman Sachs estimates that the rise in Chinese exports has already reduced goods prices by around 0.6% across major developed economies outside the US. So, China is exporting disinflation for consumers and pressure on industrial profits and jobs elsewhere. Beijing wants to fight involution, restore margins and avoid a global protectionist backlash but local governments continue to support their industrial champions in order to protect jobs and meet growth targets.

The country’s most important export today may be its model of hypercompetition.

*Nikkei link: https://t.co/woaDvf5LZx

🇫🇷 Marine Le Pen is no longer the clear first-round favourite, she is now genuinely competitive against the strongest candidates in the runoff according to latest Elabe poll (for BFMTV and La Tribune Dimanche).

📊 She is polling around 34–35.5% in almost every configuration and is projected to beat each of the four opponents tested in the second round. The most important number is probably 52.5% Le Pen vs. 47.5% Philippe. Obviously not a done deal but the fact that the candidate who currently seems best positioned to unite the centre, part of the right and part of the left is no longer automatically beating the RN.

➡️ What stands out most is the stability of Le Pen’s base as the real battle seems to be happening behind her. Philippe can rise to 20.5% but fall to 14.5% if his political space is fragmented. Mélenchon is around 14% and Glucksmann can reach 14% while Attal is closer to 12%. Unbelievable a few years ago but Le Pen’s qualification for the second round currently looks far more secure than that of any other candidate.

1️⃣ The problem for her opponents is that the traditional “republican front” against the RN is becoming much less automatic. Mélenchon voters no longer systematically transfer to a centrist candidate, LR voters can move toward Le Pen, and in a Le Pen–Mélenchon runoff a large share of centrist voters would rather abstain. Being the candidate facing the RN is no longer enough to win according to the poll.

2️⃣ On the left, the dilemma is almost the opposite as Mélenchon looks better equipped to qualify but far less capable of winning as shown by the 30.5% vs. 69.5% result against Le Pen. Glucksmann has more potential to broaden his coalition in the second round but a weaker first-round engine. As for LR, its electoral space increasingly looks squeezed between Philippe and Le Pen.

⚠️ We still need to be cautious as this remain a poll but politically, Marine Le Pen is currently the clear first-round favourite and probably the candidate with the easiest path to final victory according to betting markets.

For 30 years, the entire drop in the 10-year Treasury yield happened on the 3 days around Fed meetings. That broke in 2022. The yield has jumped about 4 points since, and almost none of it landed on a Fed day.

The bond market sets the long end now. So the next time the Fed cuts, do not expect it to pull your mortgage down or bail out long bonds. Those yields track Treasury supply and the term premium, and the Fed no longer holds that lever.

More companies are borrowing just to pay the interest on debt they already owe.

Inside the private-credit funds retail buys for yield, payment-in-kind loans, where the borrower rolls unpaid interest into the balance, have repriced up near 10.25%. Cash-paying borrowers pay around 8.3%, and the gap is widening.

tweets.text: It is a tough call and I understand both sides of the debate. My read of the situation is that the Fed is severely limited in dealing with the last 1% of inflation and - given the tools at its disposal - getting rid of that last 1% will be painful (and most likely temporary unless their is a change upstream w/ fiscal). So, I'd prefer to give max patience before moving into a new tightening regime. Just how I see it. I understand the perniciousness of inflation, but crushing large segments of the rate-sensitive economy/markets comes with its own downside (hence the "dual" mandate). From my perspective, fiscal has put the Fed in a v tough position.

Sid I usually can't disagree too much w/ your analysis and I don't really here. 

Only things I'd question was how foreseeable the mix of Iran War/SOH closure + AI ramping to this extent (analysts estimates undershot realized earnings by a historic amount outside of a recession recovery). 

I don't see the labor market as strong either...I'd classify it more as "muddle-through"...wages largely stagnant...job openings < unemployed...LFPR driving UE rate. It is weird though and AI is behind it. Residential construction has shed >10k jobs over the past four months. Yet, nonresidential specialty trades is booming (+40k jobs). So, AI demand is showing up in the labor market and elongating the cycle/rate transmission.

Beyond those issues (labor market characterization + foreseeability of the exact environment we find ourselves in), I do agree with your assessment of the situation...just disagree with the response and cost/benefit analysis of hiking again.

As always, I appreciate the thoughtfulness of your response...One of my favorite accounts here!
